title: Do long cords knot themselves?
hook: Strings were tumbled in a box for ten seconds. How often did 3 m strings come out knotted?

knows: Everyday objects have sizes, positions and amounts
doesNotKnow: that in a tumbling experiment, short 0.3 m strings showed no knots while 3 m strings knotted in about half of the trials, so long cords knot themselves when jostled

misconception: A cord only gets knotted if someone ties it, so a long cord stored loose stays untangled.
objective: Raymer and Smith (2007) tumbled one string at a time in a 30 cm box, turning once a second for ten seconds. No 0.3 m string came out knotted; 3 m strings came out knotted in 55% of trials. A longer string gives its free end more loops to weave through.

claims.text: Raymer and Smith (2007) tumbled one string at a time in a 30 cm box, turning once a second for ten seconds. No 0.3 m string came out knotted; 3 m strings came out knotted in 55% of trials. A longer string gives its free end more loops to weave through.
claims.source: Raymer & Smith 2007, Spontaneous knotting of an agitated string, doi:10.1073/pnas.0611320104, full text opened 2026-10-14 at https://www.mit.edu/~kardar/research/seminars/knots/RaymerSmithPNAS.pdf; p.16432 standard 0.30m box, 1 revolution/s, 10s, length dependence; p.16435 end weaving model. No household knot probability is asserted. FC LH-1 (session 2, received by message): verified; see company/reviews/lifehacks-200/fact-check-LH1-2026-10-14.md. Reset to unverified 2026-10-16 by demo-builder (r11 fix plan wave W3: new prediction line, stage and reveal; engine 2). Re-verify against the rebuilt stage. | FC pass 54 (fact-checker, 2026-10-16): VERIFIED. Opened Raymer and Smith 2007, PNAS 104(42):16432-7, on PMC (PMC2034230). Results: "Most of the measurements were carried out ... tumbling in a 0.30 x 0.30 x 0.30-m box rotated at one revolution per second for 10 sec"; "A string was placed in a cubic box" (one string). "No knots were obtained for L < 0.46 m", which covers 0.3 m (the text does not say whether exactly 0.3 m was among the lengths run; Fig. 2 image host cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov is blocked). Table 1: "3-m length of #4 string, tumbled at one revolution per second for 10 sec": 55% in the 0.3 m box (200 trials). Model: knotting needs "more than one coil, so that at least one segment lies adjacent to the string end", and the longest strings give "about 10-20 adjacent segments", supporting "a longer string gives its free end more loops to weave through". recall.question: In the tumbling-box study, 3 m strings knotted in 55% of trials. What does that tell you about a 3 m cable coiled in your drawer?
options: It will knot 55% of the time too
The 55% belongs to that box setup only
It cannot knot at all unless something tumbles it
recall.why: 55% is the frequency observed in a 30 cm box turning once a second for 10 seconds. A drawer is a different box, string and motion, so that number does not transfer to it as a probability.
